source_text: «ἐκτίσθην ὑπὸ τοῦ πατρός»; 16.53 ὅπερ ἀκούειν μήτιγε καὶ λέγειν φρικτὸν καὶ φευκτόν. 16.54 Οὐδαμοῦ μὲν οὖν παντελῶς θείας καὶ πνευματικῆς γραφῆς εὕρηται ταῦτα· τοὐναντίον δὲ συγκρίνοντος ἑαυτὸν πρὸς τὸν πατέρα ἐστὶν πάντα τοῦ μονογενοῦς τὰ περὶ τῆς θεότητος αὐτοῦ ῥήματα καὶ ἑνοῦντος ἑαυτὸν καὶ ὁμότιμον ἀποφαίνοντος. 16.55 ἀλλ' οὐδὲ τέκνον ἢ παιδίον ἢ γέννημα εἴρηται πώποτε κατὰ τὴν ἄνω ἄπειρον γέννησιν ἣν οὐδὲν τὸ παράπαν χαρακτηρίσαι δύναται, ἵνα μή τι μικρὸν ἢ ὑπόνοιαν παρέχον ταῖς προλεχθείσαις αὐτῶν σεσοφισμέναις βλασφημίαις φαντασθείῃ τις, ἀλλ' υἱὸς διὰ τὸ τέλειον καὶ τὸ ἀνάρχως γεννηθῆναι καὶ τὸ πρὸς τὸν πατέρα τῆς φύσεως ἀπαράλλακτον. 16.56 Ὅλα δὲ τὰ νομιζόμενα παρά τισιν εἶναι πρὸς θεότητα μικρὰ καὶ τό «ὁ πέμψας με πατὴρ μείζων μού ἐστιν» διὰ τὴν φιλάνθρωπον καὶ ἄρρητον ἐνανθρώπησιν αὐτοῦ τὴν δι' ἡμᾶς καὶ ὑπὲρ ἡμῶν γενομένην ταῖς ἱεραῖς κεχρησμῴδηται βίβλοις. 16.57 δι' ἣν καὶ ἀγγέλων ἠλαττῶσθαι γέγραπται κατὰ τὸν ἀπόστολον ἐπιστείλαντα· «τὸν δὲ βραχύ τι παρ' ἀγγέλους ἠλαττωμένον βλέπομεν Ἰησοῦν διὰ τὸ πάθη μα τοῦ θανάτου». 16.58 Ἐγὼ οὖν οἶμαι καὶ οὐ πάντως διασφάλλομαι, ὅτι περὶ τοῦ πατρὸς καὶ ἑαυτοῦ εἶπεν τὴν ἀμφοῖν δεικνὺς ἀγαθότητα καὶ ὁμοουσιότητα· «ἢ ποιήσατε τὸ δένδρον καλὸν καὶ τὸν καρπὸν αὐτοῦ καλὸν ἢ ποιήσατε τὸ δένδρον σαπρὸν καὶ τὸν καρπὸν αὐτοῦ σαπρόν· ἐκ γὰρ τοῦ καρποῦ», φησίν, «τὸ δένδρον γινώσκεται». 17.1 Ἐπειδὴ δὲ θεομαχοῦντες οἱ μὲν σὺν τῷ υἱῷ καὶ τὸ ἅγιον πνεῦμα τὸ πρῶτον κτίσμα εἶναι λέγειν τολμῶσιν, Μακεδόνιος δὲ τὸ πνεῦμα μόνον, ἐπ' ἐκείνους μὲν τὸ βάρος τοῦ ἐπιμνησθῆναι τῶν τοιούτων ἀπονενοημένων καὶ κατακρίτων ῥημάτων τρέψειεν ἡ ἁγία καὶ ὁμοούσιος τριάς, 17.2 ἡμεῖς δὲ ὑποδείξομεν τὰς θείας παρατιθέμενοι γραφὰς τὸ πρῶτον κτίσμα τοῦ θεοῦ οὕτω γεγενῆσθαι· πρῶτον κτίσμα ἐπαρθὲν ἐκ τῶν οὐρανῶν ἐρρίφη ὡς ἀστραπή, καθὰ αὐτὸς ὁ κτίσας καλῶς καὶ ὕστερον δικαίως ῥίψας ἐν εὐαγγελίῳ ἐθεώρησεν· 17.3 λέγει δὲ οὑτωσὶ παρὰ τῷ Ἰώβ· «ἀλλ' ἰδοὺ θηρίον παρά σοι χόρτον ἴσα βουσὶν ἐσθίον· ἰδού, ἡ ἰσχὺς αὐτοῦ ἐν ὀσφΰι, ἡ δὲ δύναμις αὐτοῦ ἐπ' ὀμφαλοῦ γαστρός. ἔστησεν οὐρὰν ὡς κυπά ρισσον, τὰ δὲ νεῦρα αὐτοῦ συμπέπλεκται, αἱ πλευραὶ χαλκαῖ, ὁ δὲ νῶτος αὐτοῦ σιδηροῦς χυτός. τοῦτό ἐστιν ἀρχὴ πλάσματος κυρίου πεποιημένον ἐγκαταπαίζεσθαι ὑπὸ τῶν ἀγγέλων». 17.4 ὥστε τὸν διάβολον πρῶτον κτίσμα εἶναι λέγει ἑαυτὸν ποιήσαντα ἐγκαταπαίζεσθαι ὑπὸ τῶν ἁγίων ἀγγέλων διὰ τὸ ἀνόσιον αὐτοῦ καὶ κακόβουλον τῆς προαιρέσεως. οὐκ ἂν δὲ μετ' αὐτὸν ὁ υἱὸς ὁ καὶ τοῦτον δημιουργήσας οὔτε μὴν τὸ πνεῦμα τοῦ θεοῦ ἐκτίσθη. 18.ν Περὶ τῆς ἁγίας τριάδος καὶ ὅτι διὰ τὸ ταὐτὸν τῆς οὐσίας τὰ αὐτὰ ἐπ' ἀμφο τέραις ταῖς ὑποστάσεσιν ὀνόματα λέγονται, πάρεξ τῆς πατρότητος καὶ υἱότητος καὶ τῆς ἐκπορεύσεως τοῦ πνεύματος. τοῦτο γὰρ ἴδιον ἑκάστης ὑποστάσεως ἰδίως. καὶ ὅτι ποτὲ ὁ πατήρ, ποτὲ ὁ υἱός, ποτὲ τὸ πνεῦμα προτάσ σεται. καὶ ὅτι καὶ τὸ τριαδικὸν καὶ τὸ μοναδικὸν ἐν τῇ γραφῇ δείκνυται. 18.1 Ἐκ πάντων δὴ οὖν τῶν εἰρημένων συνέστη ὡς τὰ ἐκείνων παντοίως ἀλλότρια τῆς ἀληθείας ὄντα τυγχάνει. σοφιστείας γὰρ ἔργον τὸ εὑρεσιλογεῖν, σοφίας δὲ τὸ μετ' 17 αἰδοῦς καὶ τῆς ἐναρμοττούσης ἀποδοχῆς διερευνᾶν τὰς γραφάς. 18.2 ἀναγκαῖον δὲ λοιπὸν τὰς ἀπιθάνους αὐτῶν συρφετολογίας καὶ διαμάχας παρελθόντας καὶ τῷ νοητῷ ποτίμῳ ὕδατι τοῦ ἁγίου πνεύματος τὰς ἁλμυράς, τὸ δὴ λεγόμενον, ἀποκλυσαμένους ἀκοὰς ἐπιδεῖξαι, ὅτιπερ αἱ γραφαὶ διὰ τὸ ταὐτὸν τῆς θεότητος ποτὲ μὲν μίαν τῶν θείων ὑποστάσεων, ποτὲ δὲ τὰς τρεῖς ὀνομάζουσιν, καὶ ἑκάστῃ αὐτῶν ὁμοίως τὸ ἀγαθὸν ἀπονέμουσιν, 18.3 ὡς ὅταν λέγῃ Μωϋσῆς· «ἄκουε, Ἰσραήλ, κύριος ὁ θεός σου κύριος εἷς ἐστιν», διὰ τοῦ εἰπεῖν «εἷς» δηλώσας τὴν μίαν θεότητα, διὰ δὲ τοῦ «κύριος», εἶτα «θεὸς» καὶ πάλιν «κύριος» τὴν τριάδα σημάνας, παρ' ᾗ πᾶν ἐγκόσμιον καὶ ὑπερκόσμιον ἀγαθὸν ὑπῆρξεν καὶ ὑπάρξει τοῖς ἀνθρώποις· καὶ πάλιν· «εἶπεν ὁ θεός· γενηθήτω στερέωμα, καὶ ἐποίησεν ὁ θεὸς τὸ στερέωμα, καὶ εἶδεν ὁ θεός, ὅτι καλόν»· σημειωτέον, ὅτι καὶ τρεῖς ὑποστάσεις καὶ ἑκάστην θεὸν ὀνομάζει καὶ τὴν συμφωνίαν καὶ τὴν συνεργίαν δείκνυσιν τοῦ εἰπόντος καὶ τοῦ ποιήσαντος καὶ τοῦ ἐπαινέσαντος. 18.4 Καὶ πάλιν· «προστάττει», φησίν, «ὁ θεὸς τῷ Μωϋσεῖ λέγων· λάλησον Ἀαρὼν καὶ τοῖς υἱοῖς αὐτοῦ· οὕτως εὐλογήσετε τὸν Ἰσραήλ·
pass_a_gloss: [... or the Son:] 'I was created by the Father'? 16.53 which [is] dreadful and to be fled to hear, not to say also to speak. 16.54 Nowhere then at all in divine and spiritual Scripture have these things been found; but on the contrary all the sayings of the only-begotten about his Godhead are [those] of one comparing himself to the Father and uniting himself and declaring [himself] equal in honour. 16.55 But neither has he ever been called child or little child or offspring according to the infinite generation above, which nothing at all is able to characterize, lest someone imagine something small or [something] furnishing suspicion to their sophisticated blasphemies spoken before, but son, on account of the perfect and the being begotten without beginning and the invariableness of nature toward the Father. 16.56 And all the things thought by some to be small with respect to Godhead, also the 'the Father who sent me is greater than me', have been uttered as oracles in the holy books on account of his man-loving and unspeakable becoming-man, which happened through us and on behalf of us. 16.57 On account of which it has also been written that he was made less than angels, according to the apostle who wrote: 'but the one made a little less beside angels we see, Jesus, on account of the suffering of death'. 16.58 I then think, and am not altogether mistaken, that about the Father and himself he spoke, showing the goodness and sameness of substance of both: 'either make the tree good and its fruit good, or make the tree rotten and its fruit rotten; for from the fruit,' he says, 'the tree is known'. 17.1 And since, fighting God, some dare to say that with the Son also the Holy Spirit is the first creature, and Macedonius the Spirit only, upon those may the holy and consubstantial Trinity turn the weight of making mention of such desperate and condemned sayings, 17.2 and we will show, setting beside [us] the divine Scriptures, that the first creature of God came to be thus: a first creature, having been lifted up, was hurled out of the heavens as lightning, just as the very one who created [it] well and later justly hurled [it] beheld in the Gospel; 17.3 and he says thus in Job: 'but look, a beast beside you eating grass equally with oxen; look, its strength in the loin, and its power on the navel of the belly. It set up a tail as a cypress, and its sinews have been plaited together, the ribs bronze, and its back cast iron. This is beginning of the moulding of the Lord, made to be mocked by the angels'. 17.4 So that it says the devil is first creature, having made himself to be mocked by the holy angels on account of the unholiness and evil counsel of his choice. And the Son, who fashioned this one too, would not have been created after him, nor indeed the Spirit of God. 18.ν [Chapter title:] Concerning the holy Trinity, and that on account of the sameness of the substance the same names are said of both the hypostases, except the fatherhood and sonship and the procession of the Spirit; for this [is] proper to each hypostasis properly. And that sometimes the Father, sometimes the Son, sometimes the Spirit is set first. And that both the triadic and the monadic is shown in the Scripture. 18.1 So then from all the things said it has been established that their things happen to be in every way foreign to the truth. For it is the work of sophistry to invent arguments, but of wisdom to search out the Scriptures with reverence and the fitting reception. 18.2 And it is necessary for the rest, passing by their unpersuasive sweepings-talk and fights, and with the intelligible drinkable water of the Holy Spirit having washed out the brackish, as the saying goes, hearings, to show that the Scriptures on account of the sameness of the Godhead sometimes name one of the divine hypostases, and sometimes the three, and to each of them alike allot the good, 18.3 as when Moses says: 'hear, Israel, the Lord your God is one Lord', through saying 'one' having shown the one Godhead, and through 'Lord', then 'God' and again 'Lord' having signified the Trinity, from which every in-the-world and above-the-world good has come to be and will be for men; and again: 'God said: let a firmament come to be, and God made the firmament, and God saw that [it was] good'; it is to be noted that he names both three hypostases and each God, and shows the concord and the co-working of the one who spoke and the one who made and the one who praised. 18.4 And again: 'God commands,' it says, 'Moses, saying: speak to Aaron and to his sons: thus you will bless Israel: [...]
pass_b_english: … “I was created by the Father”? That is dreadful to hear, let alone to say, and something to flee from. Nowhere at all, then, are these things found in the divine and spiritual Scripture. On the contrary, all the sayings of the Only-begotten about his Godhead are those of one who compares himself with the Father, unites himself to him and declares himself equal in honour.

Nor has he ever been called ‘child’ or ‘little child’ or ‘offspring’ with respect to his generation above, which is infinite and which nothing whatever can describe, so that no one should imagine anything small, or anything that lends colour to their sophistical blasphemies already mentioned. He is called ‘Son’, rather, because he is perfect, because he was begotten without beginning, and because his nature does not vary from the Father’s.

All the things that some think small with respect to the Godhead, including “The Father who sent me is greater than I” (John 14:28), were uttered in the sacred books because of his loving and ineffable becoming man, which took place for our sake and on our behalf. Because of it, too, it is written that he was made lower than the angels, as the Apostle writes: “But we see Jesus, made a little lower than the angels because of the suffering of death” (Hebrews 2:9).

I think, then, and I am not altogether mistaken, that it was of the Father and himself that he spoke, showing the goodness and the oneness of substance of both: “Either make the tree good and its fruit good, or make the tree rotten and its fruit rotten; for by the fruit,” he says, “the tree is known” (Matthew 12:33).

Some, fighting against God, dare to say that the Son, and with him the Holy Spirit, is the first creature, and Macedonius says this of the Spirit alone. May the holy and consubstantial Trinity turn upon them the weight of our having to mention such mad and condemned words. For our part, we shall show from the divine Scriptures we set out that the first creature of God came to be in this way. The first creature, lifted up, was hurled down from the heavens like lightning, as he who created it well, and later justly hurled it down, beheld it in the Gospel (Luke 10:18).

And he speaks thus in Job: “But behold, a beast beside you that eats grass like oxen. Behold, its strength is in its loins, and its power on the navel of its belly. It set up its tail like a cypress, and its sinews are woven together; its ribs are bronze, and its back is cast iron. This is the beginning of the Lord’s handiwork, made to be mocked by the angels” (Job 40:15-19).

So it says that the devil is the first creature, and that he made himself a thing to be mocked by the holy angels because of the unholiness and malice of his choice. The Son, who fashioned even him, would not have been created after him; nor indeed would the Spirit of God.

On the holy Trinity: that because of the sameness of substance the same names are used alike of the hypostases, except fatherhood, sonship and the procession of the Spirit, for this is proper to each hypostasis on its own; that sometimes the Father, sometimes the Son, sometimes the Spirit is placed first; and that both the threeness and the oneness are shown in Scripture.

From all that has been said, then, it is established that their teachings are in every way foreign to the truth. For it is the work of sophistry to invent quibbles, but of wisdom to search the Scriptures with reverence and with the acceptance that befits them.

It remains necessary, then, to pass over their implausible rubbish and wrangling, and, having washed out brackish ears, as the saying goes, with the fresh, intelligible water of the Holy Spirit, to show that the Scriptures, because of the sameness of the Godhead, sometimes name one of the divine hypostases and sometimes the three, and assign the good to each of them alike. So when Moses says, “Hear, Israel: the Lord your God is one Lord” (Deuteronomy 6:4), by saying “one” he showed the one Godhead, and by “Lord”, then “God”, and again “Lord”, he signified the Trinity, from whom every good in the world and above the world has come, and will come, to mankind.

And again: “God said: Let there be a firmament; and God made the firmament; and God saw that it was good” (Genesis 1:6-8). It should be noted that he names three hypostases and calls each one God, and shows the concord and co-working of the one who spoke, the one who made and the one who praised.
And again: “God commands Moses,” it says, “saying: Speak to Aaron and to his sons: Thus you shall bless Israel …” (Numbers 6:22-23)

choices.issue: Old draft garbled, broken and full of edition numbers
choices.choice: Retranslated the whole section from the Greek. The old English printed edition numbers 16.53-16.58, 17.1-17.4 and 18.1-18.4 in the reading text, turned the quoted 'I was created by the Father' into the question 'Was he created by the Father?', read ὁμότιμον (equal in honour) as 'of the same essence', ἐνανθρώπησις as 'humanity which came through us', said 'angels are made less' (16.57: he was made lower than the angels), turned οὐ πάντως διασφάλλομαι (I am not altogether mistaken) into 'I am not entirely certain', made 'those with the Son and the Holy Spirit' the first creation and laid the weight of the heretics' words on the Trinity (17.1 is a wish that the Trinity turn it on them), broke Job 40:15-19 off at 'like a plume...' and resumed it in a separate paragraph, garbled 17.4 ('he makes himself to say'), read προτάσσεται (is placed first) as 'will be preferred', ἀποκλυσαμένους ἀκοάς (having washed out the ears) as 'having uncovered the ears', and προστάττει (commands) as 'stands as protector'. References: '(Job 40:15)' widened to 40:15-19; '(Gen 1:6-10)' corrected to Genesis 1:6-8 (Didymus quotes 1:6-8 with the Greek 'and God saw that it was good' in 1:8); '(Deut 6:4)' written in full; Luke 10:18 and Numbers 6:22-23 added. Bracket filler '[he is]' removed.

choices.why: Continues the question begun in the previous section ('Or where did the Son say …'); only the words this section holds are translated, with a leading ellipsis.

choices.term: ὅπερ ἀκούειν μήτιγε καὶ λέγειν φρικτὸν καὶ φευκτόν
choices.english: That is dreadful to hear, let alone to say, and something to flee from
choices.why: μήτιγε 'not to speak of'; both adjectives kept.

choices.english: or anything that lends colour to their sophistical blasphemies
choices.why: Literally 'furnishing a suspicion to': a word that would give their blasphemies a foothold.

choices.english: for our sake and on our behalf
choices.why: διά with the accusative is 'because of / for the sake of', not 'through us' as the old draft had it.

choices.term: Ἐγὼ οὖν οἶμαι καὶ οὐ πάντως διασφάλλομαι
choices.english: I think, then, and I am not altogether mistaken
choices.why: Didymus' modest litotes; it affirms his reading rather than doubting it.

choices.term: τρέψειεν ἡ ἁγία καὶ ὁμοούσιος τριάς
choices.english: May the holy and consubstantial Trinity turn upon them
choices.why: Optative of wish: Didymus asks that the guilt of repeating such words fall on those who said them.

choices.term: οἱ μὲν σὺν τῷ υἱῷ καὶ τὸ ἅγιον πνεῦμα τὸ πρῶτον κτίσμα
choices.english: Some … say that the Son, and with him the Holy Spirit, is the first creature
choices.why: The opponents rank both as the first creature; Macedonius only the Spirit.
Passive of ἐπαίρω; in context the devil's self-exaltation before his fall. Kept plain without adding 'pride'.

choices.term: αὐτὸς ὁ κτίσας … ἐν εὐαγγελίῳ ἐθεώρησεν
choices.english: as he who created it well, and later justly hurled it down, beheld it in the Gospel (Luke 10:18)
choices.why: The Son is the creator who says 'I saw Satan fall like lightning from heaven'; Didymus' wording is kept.

choices.english: It set up its tail like a cypress
choices.why: LXX Job 40:12 (English 40:17); the old draft's 'plume' has no ground in the Greek.

choices.english: the beginning of the Lord’s handiwork
choices.why: πλάσμα 'thing moulded'; Didymus reads ἀρχή as 'first' (the devil as first creature).
The copy-text says 'both', though three hypostases are named in the same title; 'alike' keeps the sense without forcing a count (see problems).

choices.english: both the threeness and the oneness
choices.why: Abstract adjectives: the Trinity of hypostases and the unity of Godhead.

choices.term: τὰς ἁλμυράς, τὸ δὴ λεγόμενον, ἀποκλυσαμένους ἀκοάς
choices.english: having washed out brackish ears, as the saying goes
choices.why: A proverb (rinsing a salty hearing with fresh water, Plato, Phaedrus 243d); kept as an image.

choices.term: κύριος ὁ θεός σου κύριος εἷς ἐστιν
choices.english: the Lord your God is one Lord
choices.why: Didymus has σου (your) where the Septuagint has ἡμῶν (our); his wording is translated.
Didymus' own wording for Numbers 6:22 ('the Lord spoke to Moses'); kept inside his quotation marks. The section ends inside the quotation (after Ἰσραήλ·), marked with '…'.
Printed line number 17 inside the Greek is page debris and is skipped.

choices.term: πάθη μα, κυπά ρισσον, ἀμφο τέραις, προτάσ σεται
choices.why: Words split by line breaks in the copy-text; read as single words.
